description: Team of 5, 8th graders from Davis Drive Middle School with varied interests in Robotics, Aviation, Coding, AI, Mathematics.
summary:
We built an SI-powered dashboard that takes NASA’s microgravity combustion data and turns it into clear fire safety tips. We analyzed real data from NASA’s PSI database and organized the most important information, like the fuel type, oxygen flow, temperature, droplet diameter reduction and burn time. We then used the learning from the analysis dataset and created a combustion risk scoring system for these three fuel types: Solid, Liquid, and Gas.
 
The challenge asked us to make a dashboard that summarizes, ranks, and interprets NASA’s fire experiments to help keep people safe in space. Our dashboard does that by:
1) Summarizing each experiment's goal, variables, and results in a simple and easy-to-read format.
2) It ranks how risky each test is based on real data from previous NASA experiments. We assess a combustion rating of Low, Medium, or High Risk, so that people can analyze what type of conditions are most prone to cause fires and eventually dangerous situations.
3) It provides the range of certain experimental or flame parameters (eg: Oxygen flow, temperatures, burn times) for each combustion rating so that future experiments can be designed appropriately based on the risk appetite.

Our dashboard turns NASA’s complex fire data into clear and easy-to-understand risk categories, and helps scientists understand the cause of fire and identify the ways of preventing fire in space.
details:
NASA Microgravity Combustion Risk Assessment

1. Different Types of Fuel and Risk Assessment

Our project examines three types of fuel: solid, liquid, and gaseous. Since each behaves differently during combustion, we developed separate, data-informed scoring approaches to classify combustion risk as Low, Medium, or High.

We analyzed publicly available NASA experimental data to identify important combustion indicators for each fuel category.

A. Solid Fuels

  • NASA experiments: BASS-II (PSI-25) and related solid-combustion datasets.
  • Materials: PMMA, NOMEX, spherical solids, SIBAL, rod-shaped samples, and wax candles.
  • Variables: Changes in oxygen (O₂), carbon dioxide (CO₂), and carbon monoxide (CO) concentrations between the beginning and end of an experiment.
  • Assessment: Oxygen consumption and changes in CO₂ and CO are used to identify combustion-related patterns and classify risk.

B. Liquid Fuels

  • NASA experiments: FLEX and PSI-69.
  • Materials: Heptane and methanol.
  • Variables: Fuel burning rate, droplet diameter reduction, and burn time.
  • Assessment: Burning rate, fuel consumption, and combustion persistence are evaluated to determine risk.

C. Gaseous Fuels

  • NASA experiments: CFI-G and PSI-159.
  • Materials: Ethane, butane, and propane.
  • Variables: Burning rate and peak burner temperature.
  • Assessment: Both indicators are scored using ranges derived from the analyzed experimental data to classify combustion risk.

2. What Does Our Project Do, and How Does It Work?

Our project is an interactive web-based dashboard that organizes NASA microgravity combustion data and helps users explore combustion behavior across different fuel types.

NASA experiment data is often distributed across multiple experiments, reports, and datasets, making it difficult to compare results manually.

We developed a tool that:

  • Organizes relevant NASA experimental data.
  • Applies separate, rule-based scoring methods for solid, liquid, and gaseous fuels.
  • Classifies combustion risk as Low, Medium, or High.
  • Allows users to select fuel types and materials and adjust combustion parameters using interactive sliders.
  • Displays how changing individual parameters or combinations of parameters affects the risk classification.

The dashboard is built using HTML and JavaScript and hosted on GitHub.

3. What Benefits Does It Have?

Our project makes complex NASA combustion research easier to explore and understand.

Instead of manually reviewing large datasets, users can:

  • Quickly explore combustion measurements from multiple NASA experiments.
  • Compare combustion behavior across different fuel materials.
  • Understand which parameters influence combustion risk.
  • Explore with different parameter combinations through interactive sliders.

It provides an accessible educational and exploratory tool for students, researchers, and anyone interested in space and microgravity combustion.

4. What Is the Intended Impact?

Our goal is to make NASA microgravity combustion research more accessible while contributing to a better understanding of fire behavior in space.

Potential applications include:

  • Spacecraft fire safety: Helping researchers explore how different fuels and materials behave during combustion in microgravity.
  • Research and education: Making NASA experimental data easier to understand and analyze.
  • Risk assessment: Providing an initial data-informed framework to explore combustion risk under different conditions. That way proper safety measures can be put in place preemptively. 
  • Future experiment planning: Identifying important combustion parameters and combinations of conditions for further investigation.

5. What Tools Did We Use?

  • HTML and JavaScript: Building the dashboard, analyzing experimental measurements, implementing scoring rules, and displaying results.
  • GitHub: Managing the source code and hosting the website.
  • NASA public datasets: Providing experimental measurements and scientific background.
  • NIST scientific research: Understand important variables/factors for various fuel types to formulate Combustion risk
  • AI-assisted tools: ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini to help us understand scientific concepts, explore datasets, develop/debug code, AI audio using Eleven Labs to demo our tool
  • Media(Image & Video recordings): Canva Pro, Capcut

6. How Is Our Project Creative and Innovative?

Our project combines NASA experimental research, data analysis, scientific reasoning, and interactive software development into one accessible tool.

A. Finding and Filtering NASA Data

We started by identifying 26 NASA combustion-related investigations and experiments. We reviewed their available information and filtered them based on data availability and relevance to combustion risk.

This process resulted in 16 relevant investigations and experiments for further examination. Some provided usable numerical datasets, while others helped us understand important variables affecting fire behavior.

We then selected the most useful experimental datasets and organized them by fuel category.

B. Analyzing Data and Developing Risk Assessment Rules

We analyzed the selected NASA datasets to identify important combustion indicators and develop separate scoring approaches for each fuel category:

  • Solid fuels: Changes in O₂, CO₂, and CO concentrations [Figure 1 and Figure 2].
  • Liquid fuels: Burning rate, droplet diameter reduction, and burn time [Figure 3].
  • Gaseous fuels: Burning rate and peak burner temperature [Figure 4].

Using patterns and ranges observed in the experimental data, we developed our own rule-based scoring methods to classify combustion risk as Low, Medium, or High.

These are team-developed assessment rules informed by NASA experimental data, not official NASA risk ratings or universally validated fire-safety thresholds.

C. Building an Interactive Risk Assessment Tool

We implemented our scoring methods in an interactive dashboard. Users can select a fuel category and material, adjust combustion parameters using sliders, and immediately see how different conditions affect the risk classification.

This allows users to explore multiple combustion scenarios without manually analyzing the original datasets each time.

7. What Factors Did We Consider?

We considered three main factors:

  1. Availability of Data: Whether NASA experiments provided accessible, relevant measurements that could support meaningful analysis.
  2. Future Applications: Whether our findings could help researchers understand combustion behavior in space and explore spacecraft fire safety.
  3. User-Friendliness: Whether complex scientific information could be presented in a simple, interactive dashboard accessible to students and researchers.

8. Future Applications

Our project has the potential to:

  • Help researchers explore combustion behavior of different fuels in microgravity.
  • Identify combinations of parameters associated with higher combustion risk.
  • Support the planning and design of future combustion experiments.
  • Provide an interactive educational resource for students learning about space research and fire safety.
  • Expand to include additional NASA experiments, materials, and combustion indicators.

Our ultimate goal is to make complex space combustion research easier to understand and provide a foundation for further exploration of spacecraft fire safety.
